content: In anatomical terms, the arm is one of the upper limbs of an animal. Specifically, in humans, the arm refers to the segment between the shoulder and the elbow. The segment between the elbow and the wrist is called the forearm. However, in everyday language, the term arm often refers to the entire upper limb, from the shoulder to the wrist. In primates, the arms are highly specialized for climbing and performing skilled, manipulative tasks. The shoulder joint, which is a ball-and-socket joint, allows for a wide range of circular motion. Additionally, the presence of two forearm bones, the radius and ulna, which can rotate around each other, provides an extended range of motion. Anatomy of the Human Arm The human arm is composed of bones, joints, muscles, nerves, and blood vessels. Many of these muscles are essential for performing daily tasks. Bony Structure and Joints The humerus is the bone of the upper arm. It articulates with the scapula at the shoulder joint (glenohumeral joint) and with the radius and ulna at the elbow joint. Elbow Joint The elbow joint is a hinge joint formed by the distal end of the humerus and the proximal ends of the radius and ulna. The humerus is structurally robust and can withstand pressures of up to 300 pounds, making fractures uncommon. Osteofascial Compartments The arm is divided into two osteofascial compartments by a fascial layer known as the lateral and medial intermuscular septa. These compartments are: Anterior compartment of the arm: Contains muscles primarily responsible for flexion. Posterior compartment of the arm: Contains muscles primarily responsible for extension. The fascia merges with the periosteum (the outer layer of bone) of the humerus. Each compartment contains muscles innervated by the same nerve and performing similar actions. Two additional muscles are partially associated with the arm: The deltoid muscle, which is primarily located in the shoulder region, has part of its body in the anterior compartment. It is the main abductor of the upper limb. The brachioradialis muscle, which originates in the arm but inserts into the forearm, is responsible for supination, rotating the hand so the palm faces forward. Cubital Fossa The cubital fossa is a clinically significant triangular region located at the anterior aspect of the elbow. Its borders are: Laterally: The medial border of the brachioradialis muscle. Medially: The lateral border of the pronator teres muscle. Superiorly: The intercondylar line, an imaginary line between the two condyles of the humerus. Floor: The brachialis muscle. Roof: The skin and fascia of the arm and forearm. The cubital fossa contains several vital structures, which pass into the forearm in the following order from medial to lateral: 1. Median nerve: Begins to branch here. 2. Brachial artery: Supplies blood to the forearm. 3. Tendon of the biceps brachii muscle. 4. Radial nerve. 5. Median cubital vein: This vein is clinically important for venepuncture and connects the basilic and cephalic veins. 6. Lymph nodes. Nervous Supply The musculocutaneous nerve (originating from spinal nerves C5, C6, and C7) is the primary nerve supplying the muscles of the anterior compartment. It arises from the lateral cord of the brachial plexus, pierces the coracobrachialis muscle, and innervates the brachialis and biceps brachii muscles. It terminates as the anterior cutaneous nerve of the forearm. The radial nerve (originating from C5 to T1) is a continuation of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus. It enters the lower triangular space of the arm and lies deep to the triceps brachii muscle, traveling alongside the profunda brachii artery in the radial groove of the humerus. This anatomical relationship is clinically significant, as fractures of the humeral shaft can damage the radial nerve, leading to nerve lesions or transections. Other nerves passing through the arm include: The median nerve (C5-T1), which travels between the biceps and triceps muscles and enters the forearm through the cubital fossa. The ulnar nerve (C7-T1), which travels in the same plane as the median nerve but passes posterior to the medial epicondyle of the humerus at the elbow. This makes it vulnerable to injury in cases of condylar fractures. Blood Supply and Venous Drainage Arteries The primary artery of the arm is the brachial artery, a continuation of the axillary artery. The transition occurs distal to the lower border of the teres major muscle. The brachial artery gives off an important branch, the profunda brachii artery (deep artery of the arm), just below the lower border of the teres major. The brachial artery continues through the anterior compartment of the arm, traveling between the biceps and triceps muscles, accompanied by the median nerve and basilic vein. It terminates in the cubital fossa, where it divides into the radial and ulnar arteries. The profunda brachii artery travels with the radial nerve through the lower triangular space and lies deep to the triceps muscle in the spiral groove of the humerus. Fractures in this region can damage both the radial nerve and the artery, potentially causing hematomas and nerve lesions. The profunda brachii artery anastomoses with the recurrent radial branch of the brachial artery, ensuring a rich blood supply to the elbow joint. Veins The veins of the arm drain blood from the extremities and the arm itself. The two main veins are: The basilic vein, which travels medially and terminates at the level of the seventh rib. The cephalic vein, which travels laterally and terminates as the axillary vein. It passes through the deltopectoral triangle, a space between the deltoid and pectoralis major muscles. The median cubital vein, which connects the basilic and cephalic veins, is clinically significant for venepuncture. It is located in the cubital fossa.
